articles.title: The Hidden Cost of Tool Sprawl Isn't the Subscription
articles.excerpt: Tool sprawl gets budgeted like a subscription problem, and that's exactly why it keeps getting worse. Every renewal cycle, someone runs the math on a spreadsheet: forty-one SaaS tools, average $38/sea…
articles.body: Tool sprawl gets budgeted like a subscription problem, and that's exactly why it keeps getting worse. Every renewal cycle, someone runs the math on a spreadsheet: forty-one SaaS tools, average $38/seat/month, multiply by headcount, present the total as "the cost of tool sprawl," and propose consolidating six of them to shave the line item. The number is real. It's also the smallest part of what tool sprawl actually costs. The subscription is the visible cost. The compounding relationships underneath aren't. The Subscription Number Measures the Wrong Layer The per-seat price is the most visible cost of tool sprawl because it shows up cleanly on an invoice, which is precisely why it becomes the number finance sees first.
articles.author: NTCTech

articles.title: The AI App Builder Problem Nobody Talks About: What Happens After Launch?
articles.excerpt: AI app builders have gotten really good at the beginning. Describe an idea. Generate a few screens. Connect some data. Add authentication. Deploy. And suddenly you have something that looks like a rea…
articles.body: AI app builders have gotten really good at the beginning. Describe an idea. Generate a few screens. Connect some data. Add authentication. Deploy. And suddenly you have something that looks like a real product. That part is impressive. But I think we're starting to optimize for the wrong milestone. Getting an app online isn't the end of the hard part. For most products, it's where the useful questions finally begin. Launch gives you answers your prompt never could Before launch, almost everything is an assumption. You think users will understand the onboarding. You think feature A matters more than feature B. You think the pricing page makes sense. You think people will use the workflow the way you designed it. Then real users arrive. And they do something completely different.

I fixed six blind spots in my L1 regex patterns, got to 100% on the test suite, shipped v4.5.0, and wrote it up. I thought the story was over. It wasn't. What I Didn't Say in the First Article Here's what I didn't mention: v4.5.0 shipped with five advanced detectors all in alert-only mode . They could detect threats, but they didn't block anything. They logged warnings and set response headers. That's it.

articles.title: Building an Internal AI Assistant on AWS: A Production-Ready RAG Architecture with Amazon Bedrock
articles.excerpt: AI is becoming an increasingly important part of how organizations handle day to day work. But introducing AI into an organization is not just about connecting an application to an LLM and allowing pe…
articles.body: AI is becoming an increasingly important part of how organizations handle day to day work. But introducing AI into an organization is not just about connecting an application to an LLM and allowing people to start asking questions. For an internal AI assistant to be useful, it needs access to the organization's own information. It also needs authentication, access control, protection around AI input and output, logging, and a clear separation between the AI system and the people responsible for reviewing its responses. In this project, I built an internal AI assistant on AWS that allows authenticated staff to interact with an AI assistant using the organization's internal documents as its knowledge source.

articles.excerpt: Originally published on tamiz.pro. The modern software engineer faces a paradox: we have never been able to produce code faster, yet maintaining the quality of our systems has become increasingly diff…
articles.body: Originally published on tamiz.pro . The Illusion of Speed The modern software engineer faces a paradox: we have never been able to produce code faster, yet maintaining the quality of our systems has become increasingly difficult. The proliferation of AI-assisted coding tools like Copilot, Cursor, and other LLM-based agents has drastically lowered the barrier to generating syntactically correct code. For the average developer, this looks like a productivity boon. However, for senior engineers and architects, a subtle but dangerous shift is occurring.

articles.title: Asset Tracking Is Easy Until You Have to Do Something With the Data
articles.excerpt: On paper, asset tracking is simple: stick a tracker on a thing, see the thing on a map. In practice, you end up with equipment hopping between sites, pallets moving through warehouses, trucks crossing…
articles.body: On paper, asset tracking is simple: stick a tracker on a thing, see the thing on a map. In practice, you end up with equipment hopping between sites, pallets moving through warehouses, trucks crossing regions, and a few assets that need someone watching their temperature. Each of those wants a different tracking method, and getting a coordinate back is the easy part. The hard part is making that data trigger something useful. Here's how I'd approach designing one of these systems, roughly in the order I'd make decisions. Ask about the asset before you pick the tech It's tempting to start with "let's use GPS" or "let's do BLE." Resist that. Start with questions like these: What are we tracking? Where does it normally live and move: indoors, outdoors, both?

articles.title: Platform Engineering 2026: Why DevOps Alone Is No Longer Enough
articles.excerpt: Platforms Instead of Processes: Platform Engineering Solves DevOps' Scaling Problem A new engineer starts at a growing fintech company. She gets a laptop, access to the Git repository, and a Confluenc…
articles.body: Platforms Instead of Processes: Platform Engineering Solves DevOps' Scaling Problem A new engineer starts at a growing fintech company. She gets a laptop, access to the Git repository, and a Confluence page titled "Getting Started" that was last updated eleven months ago. She spends two days fighting to find the right Kubernetes cluster. A ticket for database provisioning sits in the queue for three days. She copies a CI/CD pipeline from another team's repository and spends another day figuring out why it fails in her namespace. After two weeks, she has written zero lines of business logic. This story repeats daily in companies that have reached the limits of traditional DevOps practices.

From the (alleged) $118,000 bill to AI-generated T-shirt designs, we're here to explain how a Minecraft YouTube channel has captured the internet's attention. It's a tale as old as time : a child is playing a video game, they grab their parent's credit card, and all of a sudden, someone has a thousand-dollar hole in their bank account. The story of Mighty Mike has so much in common with the lesson countless others have learned in the past – or does it? articles.title: Silent Hill: Townfall Review
articles.excerpt: Like the intravenous needle permanently jutting out of its hero’s wrist, Silent Hill: Townfall gives this long running series a welcome shot in the arm.
articles.body: I spent so much of my time stalking through Silent Hill: Townfall tensed in a cautious crouchwalk, that by the end of the story I was just as worried about the damage to my character’s fraying mental state as I was about the wear and tear on his knees. Taking an about-face from the action-heavy adventure in last year’s Silent Hill f, this latest survival horror spin-off instead embraces the sustained tension of slow-paced stealth, handing you a motion-sensing gadget and tasking you with sneaking past a series of sound-sensitive beasts that have descended on its abandoned seaside village in mid-nineties Scotland. What unfolds is a gripping investigation through an increasingly unsettling world witnessed from a fresh, first-person perspective.

Analemma over the Callanish Stones Explanation: If you went outside at the same time every day and took a picture that included the Sun , how would the Sun’s position change? A visual answer to that question is an analemma , a composite image taken from the same spot at the same time over the course of a year.
